The Internet’s Hidden Repair Constraint

Submarine cables are not fragile in the way headlines often suggest. They fail regularly, and the industry has spent decades learning how to route around damage, locate faults and repair them.

By Bottleneck Briefs · Published 2026-06-21 · Updated 2026-06-28 · 12 min read

In brief

  • 150–200 | annual telecom cable faults, mostly accidental
  • 48% | projected cable-kilometre growth by 2040
  • $3B | estimated fleet-renewal requirement
  • Three ships | ACMA’s currently disclosed regional maintenance fleet
  • 2028 | scheduled delivery year for OMS’s first new SX252 vessel

The system already fails often—and usually recovers

The International Telecommunication Union says submarine cables carry more than 99% of international data exchange and recorded more than 200 repairs worldwide in 2023. The International Cable Protection Committee estimates that the network spans roughly 500 systems and 1.8 million kilometres, with 150 to 200 telecom cable faults in a typical year. It attributes 70% to 80% of those faults to fishing and anchoring rather than hostile action. (ITU cable resilience) (ICPC cable facts)

That base rate matters. Cable length grew from about 1 million kilometres in 2014 to roughly 1.7 million kilometres in 2025, while reported annual faults remained broadly stable. Better burial, route planning and marine coordination appear to have reduced faults per kilometre.

The November 2024 Baltic incidents offer the closest recent operating test. ICPC reports that two damaged cables were restored within two weeks without service interruption. Traffic rerouting absorbed the initial shock while the physical repairs proceeded.

The United Kingdom’s 2025 parliamentary review reached a similar conclusion. Ordinary failures are generally managed efficiently, and users often do not notice an individual break because traffic shifts to surviving routes. The report found no imminent threat to national connectivity. (UK Parliament cable review)

This is the historical base rate: more cable, stable fault counts, resilient rerouting and functioning maintenance agreements. Any claim of a general repair crisis has to overcome that evidence.

The real gate is dispatchability

The narrower risk begins after redundancy has done its job.

A cable owner can reroute traffic around an isolated fault. The harder case arrives when several faults occur in one region, surviving routes lack spare capacity, or the break lies in waters where a technically capable vessel cannot operate freely.

The relevant unit is an eligible repair package: a specialist vessel, trained jointing crew, subsea tools, compatible cable and repeater spares, contractual priority, insurance, permits and territorial access. A ship without the other elements is not dispatchable capacity.

TeleGeography and Infra-Analytics project a 48% net increase in deployed cable kilometres by 2040 while roughly two-thirds of the current maintenance fleet reaches end of service. Their estimate is that about $3 billion would fund 15 replacement vessels and five additional ships needed to sustain current service levels. (TeleGeography maintenance outlook)

That is a prospective pacing risk, not proof of present scarcity. Public data do not show basin-level vessel utilization, repair queues, day rates or worsening tail restoration times. The case is strongest as a warning about future dispatchability, especially where several constraints combine.

The Strait of Hormuz illustrates that combination. Reuters reported in April 2026 that physical splicing might be routine while mines, vessel-owner risk tolerance, insurers and permissions to enter territorial waters could delay the mission. Satellites could not replace the same data volume at comparable cost. (Reuters on Hormuz)

Taiwan shows a less severe version. Bad weather prevented the coast guard from boarding a vessel suspected of damaging a cable in January 2025. Repair was scheduled for weeks later, although communications were not disrupted. The incident demonstrated attribution and maritime-access friction rather than a national connectivity failure. (Reuters on Taiwan)

The hidden constraint is therefore conditional. Repair capacity matters most after route diversity, traffic engineering and normal commercial maintenance can no longer absorb the event.

Larger cables increase consequence, not necessarily fault rates

AI and cloud demand are producing longer and higher-capacity cable systems, but that does not mechanically create more faults.

Meta’s Project Waterworth is the clearest demand-side example. The company describes a multi-billion-dollar, multi-year system extending more than 50,000 kilometres across five continents with 24 fibre pairs. It also plans deep-water routing and enhanced burial in high-risk shallow areas. (Meta Waterworth)

Google’s Firmina was designed to operate from a single power source at one end if power from other landing points becomes unavailable. That architecture protects against some failure modes while leaving physical breaks as a maintenance problem. (Google Firmina)

These designs cut both ways. Better burial and resilient power architecture may keep fault rates low. At the same time, very large systems can concentrate more traffic and strategic importance into each route.

The UK parliamentary review warned that newer high-capacity cables can become higher-value targets because more critical traffic may travel through fewer systems. The consequence of failure can rise even when the frequency of faults does not.

That distinction prevents the argument from drifting into a simple cable-growth story. More deployed kilometres are an exposure measure. The operational question is whether route diversity, terrestrial backhaul and repair readiness keep pace with the consequence attached to each new system.

The industrial base is specialized and concentrated

The cable-repair ecosystem is small because the work is unusually specific. Ordinary merchant ships cannot simply replace purpose-built cable vessels.

SubCom reports eight purpose-built cable ships and 15 submersible tools. NEC says it has laid more than 450,000 kilometres of submarine cable and provides design, manufacture, installation, testing and maintenance. Alcatel Submarine Networks combines turnkey cable-system capability with fleet-based marine operations and more than 750,000 kilometres of deployed cable. (SubCom capabilities) (NEC submarine systems)

France completed its acquisition of an 80% controlling interest in ASN on December 31, 2024. Nokia retained 20% during a planned exit process. The transaction converted an industrial supplier into a directly sovereign-controlled strategic asset. (Nokia ASN completion)

Cooperative maintenance agreements organize another part of the market. The Atlantic Cable Maintenance Agreement currently identifies three specialist ships assigned to its region, alongside depots, ROVs, technical specialists and formal mobilization procedures. Its structure pools fixed readiness costs across cable owners and converts general marine capacity into contractual access. ACMA’s public materials still contain a December 31, 2025 agreement end date, so the current post-2025 legal terms are not verified.

Private fleet renewal is also moving from announcement to construction. OMS contracted two 6,500-tonne-capacity SX252 vessels from Ulstein. Steel cutting for the first vessel, CS Resilience, began on July 7, 2026. CRIST is building the hull in Poland; Ulstein will complete outfitting and commissioning in Norway; delivery is scheduled for 2028. (Ulstein construction milestone)

The concentration is real, but it does not automatically create pricing power. Vessel ownership, construction revenue and installed kilometres reveal capability, not segment margins, utilization or durable scarcity rents.

Governments are buying readiness, not yet operating a fleet

European policy has moved beyond risk assessment, but the public-response layer remains pre-deployment.

The European Commission’s cable-security framework covers prevention, detection, response, recovery and deterrence. Its mapping work includes ownership, landing sites, incidents, maintenance, repair processes, legal constraints and supply-chain dependencies.

A 2025 proposal called for work toward an emergency repair fleet. The implemented response has been more modular. In February 2026, the Commission announced €347 million for strategic cable projects, including €20 million for adaptable repair modules positioned at ports or shipyards. The EU fleet remains a policy objective; an operational European repair fleet has not been verified.

The Commission later funded Baltic and Mediterranean Regional Cable Hubs with €5.8 million and opened a further €40 million repair-capacity call. The module specification requires applicants to identify at least three vessels capable of receiving the equipment and to support installation within three days of a vessel arriving at the designated port or shipyard. (EU hubs and repair call)

This is procurement design, not operational capacity. No verified module award, acceptance test, real dispatch or continuing availability contract has yet established that the approach works.

The United States is acting through regulation rather than emergency equipment. Provisions of the FCC’s updated submarine-cable licensing rules that depended on information-collection approval became effective on July 8, 2026. Applicants and licensees face more detailed ownership, system, capacity, landing, covered-equipment, cybersecurity and physical-security requirements. The FCC did not impose a general removal-and-replacement requirement for existing covered equipment. (FCC cable order)

These rules increase the value of trusted equipment records and regulatory visibility. They do not create a general federal approval system for every repair ship or crew.

Where value might move—and why it may not

If sovereign readiness becomes repeatable procurement, spending will not move only toward shipowners.

Public buyers would need module integrators, ports, heavy-lift capacity, secure storage, cable and repeater inventories, class approval, trained jointing crews, exercises, data-sharing platforms and maintenance contracts. Regional hubs could also create recurring work around anomaly detection, incident management, secure communications and cross-border tasking.

The strongest control point may be orchestration. A supplier that controls system design, compatible spares, marine assets, crew knowledge, regulatory provenance and maintenance priority can reduce interface risk for the customer.

Vertically integrated suppliers such as ASN, SubCom and NEC already cover much of that lifecycle. Commercial maintenance agreements retain the customer relationship and repair-priority workflow. Modular public systems may therefore complement incumbent operators instead of displacing them.

That possibility is central to the economics. The EU describes modular capacity as a backstop for cases in which the market cannot respond adequately. Existing vessel operators could provide host ships, integrate equipment, train crews and maintain the modules. Adoption may reinforce their role.

The available financial evidence also requires restraint. OMS disclosed a $400 million KKR commitment and $292.5 million of syndicated facilities before ordering new vessels. Those amounts show that an integrated marine and digital-infrastructure platform can attract capital. They are financing inflows, not cable-repair revenue.

The same caution applies to public budgets. The €20 million pilot, €40 million call and €5.8 million hub awards are separate programmes, but none should be treated as supplier sales until contracts and eligible-cost allocations identify the recipients.

The value-migration thesis remains unproven. Spending and regulatory control are beginning to move, but customer ownership, standards, data, workflow and margins may remain with incumbent cable owners and integrated maintenance suppliers.

The counterargument is stronger than the scarcity story

The best argument against the thesis is straightforward: the existing system works.

Fault counts have remained stable despite major cable growth. Rerouting usually prevents service disruption. Commercial maintenance agreements pool assets effectively. New cable designs use burial, route diversity and resilient power architecture. Private operators are ordering vessels, while the EU is developing modular alternatives.

The apparent bottleneck may also sit elsewhere. Users experience outages when surviving routes, landing stations or terrestrial networks cannot absorb traffic. Physical repairs can take weeks without causing a meaningful service loss. In those cases, spare network capacity and traffic-management coordination matter before vessel dispatch.

The first EU repair programmes could also become policy theatre. A grant award does not prove that equipment can be installed rapidly, used across several vessels, insured, crewed and dispatched into contested waters. A harbour test does not prove performance during bad weather or a live cable recovery.

Even a delivered vessel may not relieve the relevant constraint. It could replace retired tonnage, spend most of its time on installation projects or operate outside the region where clustered faults occur.

The surviving thesis is therefore narrow: an eligible repair package can become the restoration-time gate during clustered or contested-water events. The evidence does not show a present global shortage, declining ordinary repair performance or durable scarcity rents.

The next three years decide whether this becomes a market

The key transition is from grants and construction milestones to measured operational readiness.

Between 2026 and the end of 2027, the main evidence will be administrative but still useful: named EU awardees, technical annexes, selected ports, compatible vessels and module suppliers. These records will show whether governments can assemble a credible procurement package.

The stronger test arrives by the end of 2028. A module must demonstrate compatibility across at least three vessels, installation within three days and an end-to-end exercise involving cable recovery, jointing, testing and redeployment. CS Resilience is also scheduled for delivery in 2028, providing a separate test of whether private fleet renewal remains on schedule.

Repeatable commercialization requires more. By 2030, a European authority or consortium would need to sign a multi-year availability contract with a measurable mobilization service level, continuing maintenance funding and evidence that the obligation can be met.

Failure to reach those thresholds would not mean cable resilience is poor. It could mean the existing commercial system, private newbuilds and route engineering relieved the problem before a distinct sovereign market formed.

What to watch

  • October 8, 2026: whether the €40 million EU repair-module call closes without extension.
  • December 31, 2026: whether the Baltic pilot names at least one funded deployment project.
  • December 31, 2028: whether an EU module completes a three-vessel, three-day installation test.
  • December 31, 2028: whether OMS takes delivery of CS Resilience and assigns it to operational work.
  • December 31, 2030: whether Europe signs a three-year repair-availability contract with a mobilization SLA.
  • Next clustered fault: whether restoration delay is caused by dispatch constraints or inadequate rerouting capacity.

The cable system does not need to be failing today for repair readiness to matter. The decision point is whether redundancy, commercial maintenance and new vessels continue to absorb the risk—or whether a tail event exposes the missing package of vessel, crew, spares, permission and insurance.
